summary:
FIREFALL is an SI-powered dashboard that turns NASA's microgravity combustion experiments into fire-safety answers for crewed habitats. It loads all 24 combustion science investigations in NASA's Physical Science Informatics (PSI) repository, 2,009 table rows (1,879 individual tests plus test-day and other summary rows) in common units, and ranks them for a chosen habitat: the ISS cabin, a lunar base, a pressurized rover, or a Mars habitat. Every number traces back to its source file and line, and an SI assistant answers questions using only that data, with citations it checks itself.

Its headline finding: NASA expects a Moon base to run at 30 % or more oxygen at 10.2 psi or less, yet none of the 389 solid-material tests in PSI (fabrics, plastics, Nomex) records pressure, and the highest oxygen recorded is 22.2 %. NASA has burned materials at exploration-like oxygen and pressure in Saffire-IV and V, but that data is not in PSI, the open repository the challenge points to, so researchers cannot search, compare or reuse it there.
details:
What it does

Fire is one of the most dangerous hazards in spaceflight, from Apollo 1 to the Mir fire to the smoke alarm on Artemis II. NASA's fire-safety work rests on prevention, detection and suppression, and decades of experiments now sit in PSI. But the data is hard to find, harder to compare, and harder still to interpret. Our dashboard does that work:

  • Rank: scores every investigation for a target habitat on four transparent components: fire-safety pillar, closeness of its tested oxygen and pressure to the habitat's atmosphere, how directly it addresses fire safety, and data richness. Every weight is adjustable, presets serve different users (lunar base designer, modeler, equipment engineer), and each score shows how it was built.
  • Explore: a condition map of oxygen vs pressure for every test, variable-relationship plots, and a filtered export for predictive modeling.
  • Insights: key findings for lunar and Martian habitats, lessons from past spacecraft fires (Apollo 1, Apollo 13, Mir, Artemis II), what NASA research beyond PSI adds, equipment-relevant results, uses on Earth, and the NASA and partner experiments whose results could fill the gaps (FM2, SoFIE, FLARE, LUCI; SoFIE has operated on the ISS and LUCI has flown, but none of their results is in PSI yet).
  • Ask: an SI assistant (Claude) that answers only from the PSI data loaded in the dashboard. It runs exact queries for any count, cites individual test rows, and the dashboard re-checks every number in an answer against the cited data, highlighting anything it cannot verify.

How we made the data trustworthy

  • All 24 Combustion Science investigations in PSI are included. Test rows come from the 20 that publish experimental tables (22 tables), parsed into common units (O₂ fraction, kPa/psi, cm/s, mm, s); the other 4 are analysis and modeling studies with no experimental table.
  • Every value keeps its source file and line. Problems in NASA's spreadsheets (impossible percentages, ambiguous numbers like "037 mm", text in numeric columns) are flagged and left empty rather than silently "fixed"; where a value is clearly recoverable (e.g. "3400%" in a column of percentages), it is recovered and marked approximate.
  • Ambient vs burner oxygen. In ACME's inverse flames (CFI-G and Flame Design, 274 tests), the oxygen value describes gas flowing out of the burner into a fuel-filled chamber, not the surrounding atmosphere. We store it separately so it is never mistaken for a habitat atmosphere. Without this, an 85 % oxygen burner stream would look like a test of an oxygen-rich cabin.
  • One non-combustion investigation was added as context: the Aerosol Sampling Experiment (cabin dust on the ISS), because background particles are what smoke detectors must not mistake for smoke.

What we found

  1. No cabin material in PSI has been tested in a lunar-habitat atmosphere. Of 389 solid-material tests, 0 record pressure and the highest oxygen is 22.2 %. The nearest tests to a lunar base atmosphere are liquid-droplet (FLEX) and gas-flame (ACME CFI-G) experiments. NASA's SoFIE facility (10–40 % oxygen at 0.2–1.5 atm) and FM2 (on the Moon) are designed to close this gap; neither has data in PSI yet. Saffire-IV and V already burned materials at exploration-like pressures and oxygen levels (https://www.nasa.gov/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/spacecraft-fire-safety-demonstration-saffire.pdf); adding those results to PSI would close much of the gap with data NASA already has.
  2. Earth-gravity screening may not be the worst case. The challenge suggests microgravity and 1 g results could bracket lunar and Martian gravity. Saffire-II is the only PSI table that reports both a microgravity and a 1 g result for the same materials: in all 8 comparable samples, 1 g burned at least as much as microgravity. That makes 1 g look like a ceiling. But NASA's own Researcher's Guide reports that the standard 1 g screening test, NASA-STD-6001 Test 1, "is not conservative" (p. 31), and NASA researchers report that flame spread peaks and the oxygen needed to sustain a flame is lowest near lunar gravity. Our dashboard shows both, so designers don't treat 1 g as a safe upper bound.
  3. There is no partial-gravity combustion data in PSI yet. This is the gap that NASA's FM2 and LUCI experiments are designed to fill. LUCI has already flown on a spinning New Shepard rocket, the first extended-duration combustion tests in simulated lunar gravity; when its results reach PSI, they can be added in the same format.

Why it matters

Artemis habitats and rovers will use a higher-oxygen, lower-pressure atmosphere that makes materials more flammable, in a gravity level where fire may behave worst. Our tool tells engineers which existing evidence applies, how close it is to their conditions, and where the evidence stops. On Earth, the challenge brief points to fine-water-mist extinguishers developed for the ISS, NASA Spinoff records better smoke detectors, firefighter air tanks and firefighter clothing, and PSI's own records point to fire safety in submarines, aircraft and mines.

Tools

Single-file HTML/JavaScript dashboard (no build step; works offline except the SI assistant), hosted on GitHub Pages; a Python validator (standard library only) that re-checks the dataset; Claude (Anthropic) for the SI assistant and development help; GitHub for collaboration.

How to check our work

Every number above can be reproduced: run python tools/verify_claims.py in our repository. It recomputes each figure from the dataset and checks every DOI against psi.nasa.gov.

Use of SI

The challenge calls AI tools Super Intelligence (SI). The SI tools we used were Claude (Anthropic) and, for one review, ChatGPT (OpenAI). No other SI tools were used.

  • In the product: the Ask tab uses Claude (Anthropic), an AI model, to answer questions. It is instructed to use only the PSI data loaded in the dashboard, and the dashboard checks every number and citation in each answer against that data and highlights anything unverified. The three example answers on the Ask tab were pre-generated by Claude from the same data and are labelled as such.
  • Building the original dashboard: a team member built the first version of the dashboard, including its data ingestion, with Claude.
  • Development during the hackathon: Claude was used to review the dashboard; fix data handling (separating burner-stream from ambient oxygen, recovering two approximate ACME BRE values); add the 0 g vs 1 g panel, key findings, past-fires, outside-research and follow-on-experiments panels and the example answers; write the data validator and exports; verify sources; and draft the documentation, this project text and the demo deck.
  • Review: teammates used Claude and ChatGPT (OpenAI) for independent pre-submission reviews. Their findings were checked against the data and sources before any change was made.
  • Where it is acknowledged: the README ("Use of SI (AI)"), the metadata of index.html, data/psi_data.json ("provenance") and data/README.md, the demo deck (slide 6 caption and PDF properties), and the repository description.
  • No data was generated by AI: every value comes from NASA's files and keeps its source file and line. No AI-generated images are used; the screenshots are of the dashboard. No SI-generated content uses NASA logos, flags or mission identifiers.
